title: The Supreme Court of Japan
hook: Japan's top court has the power of constitutional review and almost never uses it: roughly ten laws struck down in eighty years, against 900-plus in the United States.
key_points: Fifteen justices sit in three 'petty benches' of five; the full Grand Bench convenes only for exceptionally important cases.
An informal quota divides seats among career judges, prosecutors, bureaucrats, private lawyers and law professors — judges and prosecutors always hold the majority.
Justices retire at 70 and face a voter retention review at the next legislative election; none has ever come close to being removed.
The court decides roughly 10,000 cases a year, mostly by summary disposition; the US Supreme Court decides 60–70.
In about 80 years it has invalidated maybe ten statutes, versus 900+ in the US and 600+ in Germany — and the Diet largely ignored its big 1976 malapportionment ruling.
Its research judges are career judges chosen for expertise, not clerks hired by individual justices — a check on the bench that may also mute dissent.
content_html: Japan's Supreme Court, created under the 1947 constitution, looks on paper like a powerful institution: fifteen justices with the authority to strike down laws that violate the constitution. In practice, it may be the most restrained constitutional court in any major democracy. In an interview with SCOTUSblog's Zachary Shemtob, comparative-law scholar David S. Law describes a court that has invalidated perhaps ten statutes in eighty years.
extra_html:
The structure explains a lot. The fifteen justices normally sit in three fixed five-member "petty benches," with all fifteen convening as the Grand Bench only for exceptionally weighty cases; opinions are assigned mechanically on rotation rather than chosen. Justices are formally appointed by the emperor on the cabinet's advice, but an informal quota parcels seats out among career judges, prosecutors, bureaucrats, private attorneys and law professors — and career judges and prosecutors always form the majority. The chief justice, by long practice always a career judge, wields what Law calls exceptional administrative power over judicial assignments nationwide. Justices leave at the mandatory retirement age of 70 and face a voter retention review at the first legislative election after appointment, a check Law notes has never come close to unseating anyone.

The workload is a different world too. The court disposes of roughly 10,000 cases a year, overwhelmingly through summary rulings, where the US Supreme Court decides 60 to 70. Most of the statutes it has struck down involved comparatively minor matters such as postal liability or forest subdivision rules; the major exception, a 1976 decision on electoral malapportionment, was largely ignored by the Diet. Even the clerkship system differs: "research judges" are career judges selected for subject expertise rather than staff attached to individual justices, which Law describes as a genuine check on the bench — and possibly a reason less conservative members write fewer dissents. For anyone comparing courts, it is a reminder that formal powers on paper tell you much less than who sits, how they got there, and what happens when they say no.

related.title: The Constitutional Court of South Africa
related.hook: Born out of the end of apartheid, this court was designed to make a new constitution stick — and became one of the world's most-cited voices on what rights a government owes its people.

related.title: The European Court of Justice
related.hook: A court above nations: it doesn't replace any country's supreme court, but it makes sure EU law means the same thing in every member state.

flashcards.prompt: What most distinguishes Japan's Supreme Court from other high courts with constitutional review powers?

choices.text: It almost never strikes down legislation — roughly ten statutes in about 80 years
It has no power to review the constitutionality of laws at all
Its justices are directly elected by voters to fixed terms

flashcards.explanation_html: The formal power exists; the court simply exercises it very rarely — about ten invalidations, compared with 900+ in the US and 600+ in Germany.

flashcards.prompt: How can a court have real constitutional power on paper and almost none in practice?
flashcards.back_html: Composition and habit. Career judges and prosecutors always hold the majority, the chief justice controls judicial assignments nationwide, and even a landmark ruling can be ignored — as the Diet largely did with the 1976 malapportionment decision.

flashcards.prompt: Japan's justices face a retention review by voters. What has that accomplished?

choices.text: Essentially nothing — no justice has ever come close to being voted out
It removes roughly one justice per election cycle
It replaced the mandatory retirement age of 70

flashcards.explanation_html: The review happens at the first legislative election after appointment, but it has never seriously threatened a justice — accountability on paper rather than in practice.
